verdict: Caution: lend selectively to converters with pass-through pricing and tight working-capital control; avoid commodity moulders exposed to Delhi's slower GST and power demand.
title: Narela-Bawana Plastics & Rubber Processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A plastics or rubber unit here buys resin or scrap, runs it through moulding, extrusion or reclaim lines, and sells parts or granules to nearby OEMs and traders.** Cash is made on conversion margin, not on the polymer: the resin is a pass-through, so the spread between input cost and selling price per kg is the whole business. **Value sits in the machine hours and the customer approval, not in the shed.** So when a proposal lands, ask for the per-kg conversion margin and the top five customers' share; if one buyer is above a third of sales, ask for the supply agreement and payment history.

## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Working capital is the real loan: inventory of resin and finished parts plus receivables, net of supplier credit.** Rating commentary on a peer converter shows raw material concentration is normal, with about 84% of FY25 requirements from the top five suppliers [9], so supplier terms drive the cycle. **Delhi is running slower than India: GST collections +2.7% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, and electricity demand +6.5% against +9.5% [D].** That is a local demand signal, not a national one. Nationally the industry is strong: IIP for rubber and plastics output is +21.4% YoY and +18.2% Apr-to-date [D]. **Read this as a national upcycle with a soft local market, so lend to units selling outside Delhi.**

## What peers tell us
**Peer results are healthy and recent.** Supreme Industries grew sales tonnage 19% YoY with operating profit up 45% [4]; Apcotex posted record H1 with revenue up 44% [5]; GRP's total income rose 26% with EBITDA margin at 11% [2]. GRP's earlier call guided reclaim volume growth of about 5% for FY26, accelerating to mid-teens in FY27 [3]. **The margin expansion is in specialised and reclaim grades, not plain commodity moulding.** Note the sources say nothing specific about Narela-Bawana itself; the landfill news [1] is undated and carries no lending signal, so lean on first principles and these peers.

## Who to pursue now, and how to grow safely
**Pursue reclaim-rubber and recycled-compound makers, and converters with approved-vendor status at auto or appliance OEMs.** Avoid plain commodity moulders selling to local traders on open credit. **Structure as a cash-flow loan against a drawing-power limit, not a term loan for sheds.** Take monthly stock-and-debtor statements, quarterly GST returns, and a charge on receivables; covenant that conversion margin per kg does not fall below the sanctioned base. **Ask for the power bill every month: electricity consumption is the honest production proxy.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch debtor days stretching beyond the sanctioned cycle, inventory of slow-moving grades building, and power consumption falling while sales are reported flat.** If GST turnover trails bank credits, stop enhancement and ask for the reason in writing. If a single customer crosses a third of sales, seek a tripartite arrangement or reduce exposure.
watch: turnover below credits for two months -> freeze limit enhancement and seek explanation
units fall while sales flat -> inspect stock and cut drawing power
beyond sanctioned cycle -> move to cash-and-carry on new dispatches
above one-third of sales -> seek supply agreement or reduce exposure
below sanctioned base -> reprice or exit at renewal
